passage:
Warden's note, Boys' Hostel B, 20 July
Rahil, second year, came to me asking if he could skip the mess and cook instant noodles in his room to "save money". He has also been walking forty minutes to college instead of taking the bus, for the same reason.
Last week, though, his internship bonus came through, and within days he had bought new headphones and a gaming chair, and treated the whole floor to dinner. When I asked, he said, "That was bonus money, ma'am. The bus fare comes from my real money."
He honestly doesn't see it as one pot. I didn't lecture. I asked him to write every rupee he has, from anywhere, on one sheet. His classmate Deepika, who keeps a simple notebook budget, offered to sit with him. They will meet on Sunday. I'll check in next week.
Farida

qa.q: What did Rahil buy after the internship bonus came through?
qa.a: He bought new headphones and a gaming chair, and treated the whole floor to dinner.

qa.q: Why does walking forty minutes feel sensible to Rahil while the gaming chair doesn't feel wasteful?
qa.a: Rahil feels relaxed about spending the bonus because in his mind it is a separate extra pot, while he feels protective of his "real money" and guards the bus fare tightly.

qa.q: What does Farida's one-sheet idea help Rahil see?
qa.a: Writing every rupee on one sheet shows all his money as one pot, so he can see the bonus could have covered a lot of bus rides and mess meals.

qa.q: How might Deepika see Rahil's habits when they sit together?
qa.a: Deepika may find it surprising that someone skipping the bus to save money just spent so much on a chair, and will probably help Rahil see it as one budget.

grounding: It shows a male student spending a bonus freely while pinching on bus fare and meals, because separate mental pots hide his whole picture.

passage:
Wednesday, 9 pm
Had dry bread and tea for dinner again to save forty rupees on the mess extra. I've been proud of this streak. I also skipped photocopying the notes and took photos instead, to save ten.
Then I opened my bank app to check something and saw it: the tax refund from my summer job came in three weeks ago, and I've spent almost all of it. New sneakers. A concert ticket. Snacks for everyone at Tanuja's birthday. I barely remember deciding any of it. It just felt like bonus money, not "mine".
Nikita didi called and I told her. She laughed and said, "Little brother, you're guarding coins and throwing notes." She's right. It's all one wallet.
Tomorrow: one list of everything, refund included.
Aniket

qa.q: What came into Aniket's account three weeks ago?
qa.a: The tax refund from the summer job came in three weeks ago.

qa.q: Why did the refund not feel like Aniket's own money?
qa.a: The refund felt like bonus money, so Aniket spent it carelessly without guilt, while saving forty rupees on dinner made him feel proud of his careful effort.

qa.q: Is Aniket's plan for tomorrow a good start?
qa.a: Yes; putting everything, refund included, on one list lets Aniket see the whole picture and notice the snacks and sneakers cost far more than the savings on meals.

qa.q: What does Nikita didi's line about coins and notes show about how she sees it?
qa.a: She sees the mismatch clearly and finds it a bit funny, but cares enough to point out that all the money comes from one wallet.

grounding: It shows a young man spending a tax refund carelessly while pinching on small daily costs, because he keeps the money in separate mental accounts.

passage: In the small town of Malegaon, Asif, twenty, counted every coin of his daily money. He walked three kilometres to college to save the ten-rupee shared auto, and he told Karthik, his friend from the repair shop where they both worked evenings, that chai at the stall was a luxury. Then the shop owner gave them each an Eid bonus of four thousand rupees. Asif spent his in a week: a big speaker, biryani for six friends, and a day trip to the dam on hired bikes. "Bonus money," he said. "It's extra." In March the exam form fee came due. Asif stood at the college window eight hundred rupees short and borrowed from Karthik, who had quietly kept his bonus aside.

qa.q: How far did Asif walk to college to save the auto fare?
qa.a: He walked three kilometres to save the ten-rupee shared auto.

qa.q: Why did spending the bonus in a week feel fine to Asif?
qa.a: He thought of it as "extra", separate from the daily money he guarded, so it didn't feel like part of his real budget.

qa.q: What could Asif try the next time a bonus arrives?
qa.a: He could look at all his money together, including coming costs like the exam fee, before deciding what the bonus is for.

qa.q: How might Karthik feel lending Asif money for the exam form?
qa.a: Karthik may be glad to help a friend but also a little surprised, having watched Asif fuss over ten-rupee autos and then spend a whole bonus in a week.

grounding: A young man pinches coins on daily costs but spends a bonus freely, and the separate mental pots leave him short when a fee comes due.

passage: In Lyon, Bao kept a tiny notebook of daily costs. He refused the coffee after lectures, carried his lunch in a jar and walked forty minutes to avoid buying a tram ticket. "Every cent counts," he told Ines. Then in June a tax refund of six hundred euros landed, from his part-time job at a bookshop. That wasn't in the notebook. By the end of the month it had become a weekend in Barcelona, a leather jacket and new headphones. "It's refund money," he said when Ines raised an eyebrow. "Free money." In August the rent went up, and the notebook showed Bao three hundred euros short. He stared at the neat list of saved coffees and felt foolish.

qa.q: How much was Bao's tax refund?
qa.a: A tax refund of six hundred euros.

qa.q: Why did Bao call the refund "free money"?
qa.a: It wasn't part of the notebook he tracked so carefully, so it felt separate from his real budget and easy to spend.

qa.q: What turning point shows Bao the problem, and what could he change?
qa.a: Finding himself short when the rent went up; he could put every euro, refunds included, into the same notebook so he sees the whole picture.

qa.q: What might Ines have been thinking on raising an eyebrow?
qa.a: Ines probably found it odd that someone who walked forty minutes to save a tram ticket would spend six hundred euros in a month.

grounding: A student saves small daily amounts but spends a tax refund carelessly, because keeping it in a separate mental account hides his whole situation.
